core_claim.quote: The experience of seeing occurs when the organism masters what we call the governing laws of sensorimotor contingency.

source.citation: O'Regan JK, Noë A. A sensorimotor account of vision and visual consciousness. Behavioral and Brain Sciences 24(5):939-973 (target article), with open peer commentary and the authors' response, 973-1031, 2001

prediction.statement: When goggles turn the visual world upside down or left to right, the experience of seeing comes right piece by piece, one activity at a time, as the wearer relearns how sight changes with movement: during adaptation one aspect of a scene can look right while another in the same place still looks reversed, and in the end (about two weeks of wearing) the world looks normal again.

first_stated.passage: An observer adapting to an inverted world will in the course of adaptation only be able to progressively probe subsets of the sensorimotor contingencies that characterize his or her new visual world; and so inconsistencies and contradictions may easily arise between “islands” of visuo-motor behavior.

source.citation: O'Regan JK, Noë A. A sensorimotor account of vision and visual consciousness. Behavioral and Brain Sciences 24(5):939-973 (target article), with open peer commentary and the authors' response, 973-1031, 2001

prediction.test_for: Wearers of inverting or reversing goggles report, during adaptation, that some aspects of a scene look the right way round while others in the same place still look reversed, with adaptation tied to the activities they practised; and with long enough wear they report that the world looks normal (not merely that they can act correctly in it).
prediction.test_against: Wearers learn to act normally but report that what they see stays reversed throughout, however long they wear the goggles; or the whole scene's look flips at once, as one unit, rather than aspect by aspect.

other_statements_of_the_prediction.passage: Ultimately (after about two weeks of wearing the apparatus) they come to feel that their new visual world is “normal” again.

source.citation: O'Regan JK, Noë A. A sensorimotor account of vision and visual consciousness. Behavioral and Brain Sciences 24(5):939-973 (target article), with open peer commentary and the authors' response, 973-1031, 2001

other_statements_of_the_prediction.passage: Consider, for example, someone who is adapted to reversing goggles and someone who has just put them on. These two individuals will agree in their input-output relations but they will not agree in experience.
